concepts.name: Clarify requirements and scale before designing
API, data model and high-level diagram
Designing a URL shortener's short codes

questions.prompt: The interviewer says "Design a URL shortener." What should you do first?

choices.text: Draw the load balancer, web servers and database, then ask what's missing
Pick the database first, since the schema and every other component depend on that choice
Ask who uses it, how many links per month, and the read-to-write ratio
Write the code that hashes a long URL into a short code, since that's the core feature

questions.explanation: The System Design Primer's first step is to outline use cases, constraints and assumptions: who uses it, how many users, how much data, how many requests per second, and the read-to-write ratio. Those numbers decide the rest, such as whether you need caching or sharding, so a design drawn before them is a guess.

sources.title: GitHub - donnemartin/system-design-primer: Learn how to design large-scale systems. Prep for the system design interview.
sources.claim: Step 1 of the Primer's interview approach is to outline use cases, constraints and assumptions by asking who uses the system, how much data and traffic, and the expected read-to-write ratio.

questions.prompt: Name the functional and non-functional requirements you would clarify for a URL shortener, and for each say how the answer would change the design.

model_answer.summary: Clarify what the product must do (create, redirect, expiry, custom aliases, analytics) and how well (scale, read-to-write ratio, latency, availability), because each answer adds or removes components.
key_points: Functional: create a short link and redirect to the long URL; ask whether links expire, whether custom aliases are allowed, and whether clicks are counted
Expiry needs an expiry field and a way to clean up or ignore expired links
Scale: new links per month and the read-to-write ratio set storage size and requests per second
A read-heavy ratio points to caching popular links in front of the database
Redirect latency and availability targets decide how much you replicate and cache

questions.explanation: Requirements turn a vague prompt into a problem with numbers. Interviewers expect you to ask, and to use the answers: each requirement should point to a piece of the design, not sit in a list.

sources.title: GitHub - donnemartin/system-design-primer: Learn how to design large-scale systems. Prep for the system design interview.
sources.claim: The Primer's first step gathers requirements such as users, scale, data volume and read-to-write ratio, which then drive the high-level design and scaling choices.

sources.title: Design Pastebin.com (or Bit.ly)
sources.claim: The Pastebin/Bit.ly solution lists use cases including expiring links and constraints such as a 10:1 read-to-write ratio, and its data model stores an expiration length per link.

retired.reason: Written Questions are legacy (ADR-0008): replaced by a multiple-select Question on the same Concept.

questions.prompt: The service creates 100 million short links a month. Using the rule of thumb that a month has about 2.5 million seconds, roughly how many writes per second is that on average?

choices.text: About 4
About 40
About 400
About 4,000

questions.explanation: 100,000,000 / 2,500,000 = 40 writes per second on average. The Primer's handy conversion is that 1 request per second is about 2.5 million requests a month, so 40 per second is 100 million a month. Peaks are higher than the average, so say that out loud too.

sources.title: Design Pastebin.com (or Bit.ly)
sources.claim: The solution uses the conversion of about 2.5 million seconds per month for back-of-envelope request rates, so 100 million writes a month is about 40 per second.

questions.prompt: Each short link record takes about 500 bytes. At 100 million new links a month, about how much storage do you need for 5 years?

choices.text: About 36 GB
About 300 GB
About 30 TB
About 3 TB

questions.explanation: 100 million x 500 bytes = 50 GB a month. Five years is 60 months, and 60 x 50 GB = 3,000 GB, about 3 TB. That fits comfortably in one database with replicas, which tells you sharding isn't the first problem to solve.

sources.title: Design Pastebin.com (or Bit.ly)
sources.claim: The solution estimates storage as records per month times record size and extends it over years; here 100M x 500 B = 50 GB/month, times 60 months = about 3 TB.

questions.prompt: What is the best primary key for the URL shortener's main table?

choices.text: The short code, because every redirect looks a link up by it
The long URL, because it's unique per link
The creation timestamp, so rows are stored in order
An auto-increment ID, with no index on the short code

questions.explanation: Design the data model around the hot query. Redirects vastly outnumber creations and always look up by short code, so the Primer's similar Pastebin design makes the 7-character shortlink the primary key. Long URLs aren't necessarily unique, and a table without an index on the short code would scan on every redirect.

sources.title: Design Pastebin.com (or Bit.ly)
sources.claim: The Pastebin/Bit.ly schema declares shortlink char(7) NOT NULL and makes it the PRIMARY KEY of the pastes table.

questions.prompt: Sketch the API, the data model and the high-level components of a URL shortener, and explain how a redirect request flows through them.

model_answer.summary: Two endpoints (create and redirect), one table keyed by short code, and stateless web servers behind a load balancer with a cache in front of the database.
key_points: A `POST` endpoint takes the long URL (and optional expiry) and returns the short code
A `GET /{code}` endpoint looks up the code and redirects to the long URL
The table is keyed by short code and stores the long URL, creation time and expiry
Clients reach stateless web servers through a load balancer
A redirect checks the cache first and reads the database only on a miss

questions.explanation: This matches the Primer's second and third steps: a high-level design with the important components, then the core pieces in detail. Keep the diagram tied to the numbers: the cache is there because reads dominate.

sources.title: Design Pastebin.com (or Bit.ly)
sources.claim: The solution's design has a write API that returns a shortlink, a read API that looks up the shortlink, a table keyed by shortlink with creation time and expiration, and a memory cache plus read replicas behind load-balanced web servers.

questions.prompt: Short codes are 7 characters of Base62 (`a-z`, `A-Z`, `0-9`). About how many distinct codes is that?

choices.text: About 57 billion
About 3.5 trillion
About 7 quadrillion

questions.explanation: Each position has 62 options, so there are 62^7 = 3,521,614,606,208 codes, about 3.5 trillion. 57 billion is 62^6. At 100 million links a month, 3.5 trillion lasts thousands of years, so 7 characters is plenty.

sources.title: Design Pastebin.com (or Bit.ly)
sources.claim: The solution Base62-encodes shortlinks and keeps 7 characters; 62^7 = 3,521,614,606,208 (about 3.5 trillion) while 62^6 is about 56.8 billion.

questions.prompt: You make short codes by taking an MD5 hash, Base62-encoding it and keeping the first 7 characters. What must you still handle?

choices.text: Collisions: a truncated hash can repeat, so detect the duplicate key on insert and retry
Nothing: MD5 is collision-free, so the first 7 characters of it are always unique too
Decoding: you must be able to reverse the code back into the long URL without a lookup
Case: Base62 codes must be lowercased before storing, or lookups will miss mixed-case codes

questions.explanation: Keeping only 7 characters of a hash throws most of it away, so different inputs can end up with the same code. With the short code as the primary key, a duplicate insert fails, and you retry with a changed input (for example adding a salt or timestamp). Codes are looked up, never decoded, and Base62 relies on case to reach 62 symbols.

sources.title: Design Pastebin.com (or Bit.ly)
sources.claim: The solution builds shortlinks by MD5-hashing input, Base62-encoding it and taking the first 7 characters, then checks the database and generates another URL if it is not unique.

questions.prompt: The shortener sees 100 reads for every write, and the database is the bottleneck. What is the most effective first change?

choices.text: Shard the database by the first letter of the code
Move from SQL to a NoSQL database
Make the short codes longer
Cache popular codes in memory and add read replicas for the rest

questions.explanation: The Primer's fourth step is to find the bottleneck given the constraints. With reads 100 times more common than writes and a few links very popular, a cache in front of the database absorbs most redirects, and read replicas spread the remaining reads. 3 TB doesn't yet call for sharding, which adds much more complexity.

sources.title: Design Pastebin.com (or Bit.ly)
sources.claim: For the read-heavy workload the solution recommends a memory cache for popular content and SQL read replicas for cache misses, leaving sharding and federation for write scaling.

sources.title: GitHub - donnemartin/system-design-primer: Learn how to design large-scale systems. Prep for the system design interview.
sources.claim: Step 4 of the Primer's approach is to identify and address bottlenecks given the constraints.

questions.prompt: Compare generating short codes by hashing with generating them from an incrementing counter encoded in Base62. When would you choose each?

model_answer.summary: Hashing needs no shared state but must handle collisions; a counter never collides but produces guessable codes and needs coordination across servers.
key_points: Hashing can run on any server with no shared state
Truncated hashes can collide, so inserts must check for duplicates and retry
A counter gives every link a unique number, so its Base62 codes never collide
Counter-based codes are sequential, so anyone can guess and enumerate other links
A single counter is a coordination point; servers can each reserve ranges of numbers to avoid it

questions.explanation: Interviewers want the trade-off, not a winner. If links may be private, guessable codes are a real problem and favour hashing or random codes; if simplicity and zero collisions matter more, a counter with pre-allocated ranges is fine.

sources.title: Design Pastebin.com (or Bit.ly)
sources.claim: The hash-based approach truncates an MD5/Base62 value to 7 characters, so the solution must check for duplicates and regenerate on collision.

questions.prompt: Which requirements influence a URL shortener’s design? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Whether links expire.
Only the name of the chosen database.
The expected read-to-write ratio.
The editor used to write the service.
The target redirect latency.

questions.explanation: A: Expiry changes link storage and expiration handling. B: Technology selection follows requirements; its name is not a product requirement. C: Read-heavy traffic motivates caching and capacity planning. D: An editor does not determine the service’s requirements or architecture. E: Latency targets influence caching and replication.

questions.prompt: Which components fit the Primer’s shortlink design? Select all that apply.

choices.text: A create API that requires the client to write the database directly.
A table mapping each short code to its long URL.
A redirect path that creates a new short code on every read.
A write API that returns a shortlink.
A cache lookup before the persistent lookup on a read miss.

questions.explanation: A: The service owns its write API and persistence. B: The shortlink is the lookup key. C: Reading resolves an existing shortlink rather than issuing another. D: The documented write API creates and returns the link. E: Cache-aside uses the database on a miss.

questions.prompt: In the Primer’s truncated-hash shortlink design, which steps address collisions? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Check whether a generated shortlink already exists.
Assume seven Base62 characters guarantee collision-free hashing.
Generate another candidate when a collision occurs.
Treat truncation as reducing the available code space.
Overwrite an existing mapping whenever the hash repeats.

questions.explanation: A: The documented algorithm checks duplicates. B: A finite truncated hash space can produce collisions. C: The solution retries with another generated value. D: Shortening the hash reduces the number of possible distinct codes. E: Overwriting would redirect the earlier link to the wrong resource.
